newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-LEHMAN SHOWS FORM WITH FIVE-STROKE WIN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEHMAN SHOWS FORM WITH FIVE-STROKE WIN.

text.p: Tom Lehman sprinted away from the pack with three successive birdies from the seventh to win the Loch Lomond World Invitational on Saturday in an ideal tune-up for his British Open title defence next week.
The 38-year-old American's fourth round in the 60s, this time a four-under-par 67, gave him victory by five strokes over U.S. Open champion Ernie Els.
"All parts of my game were clicking. Everything about my game was under control and solid," he said.
"I might have made a few more short putts, but then I made some long one. This has been a very fulfilling week for me."

Lehman will tackle Royal Troon next week with his confidence sky-high as he attempts to follow his success at Royal Lytham last year and become the first player since Tom Watson in 1983 to retain the British Open title.
He finished with a 19-under-par total of 265 over the exquisite 7,050-yard layout beside the bonny banks of the renowned Scottish lake.
Els closed with a five-under-par 66 to finish 14 under par on 270.
Another South African, Retief Goosen, broke the three-day-old course record by one stroke with a nine-under-par 62 to take third place two shots behind Els on 272.
Paul Curry of England and Joakim Haeggman of Sweden set the previous record of 63 in Wednesday's opening round.
Pierre Fulke of Sweden, second overnight, dropped to a fourth place tie after a 73 which left him level on 273 with world number two Greg Norman, who closed with a 68.

American Payne Stewart, who finished one shot away from the 1989 playoff when the Open was last played at Royal Troon, finished joint sixth with Mats Hallberg of Sweden and Englishman Paul Broadhurst, like Stewart a former Ryder Cup player.
Last year's U.S. Open champion Steve Jones finished alone on nine under after a 73.
"To play that well four straight days, that's not something you do very often," said Lehman, whose put together rounds of 65-66-67-67.
"To have only two bogeys in 72 holes is something I've never done before."
Lehman began the last day with a two-shot lead but that had gone when Fulke birdied the long third and Lehman bogeyed it after hitting his second shot into a bunker.
They were still level after six but Lehman took charge at the tough seventh which runs into a corner of the course beside the lake.
He hit a 170-yard six-iron approach that went under one tree and over another to 25 feet from the flag and holed the putt.
He holed from 12 feet after an eight-iron at the 155-yard eighth and from the same distance at the ninth.
After a fourth birdie at the 13th he made yet one more 12-footer for birdie at the 16th.
"I always seem to play well from the seventh but the one at 16 was the key for me. It gave me some breathing space because Ernie had just made three successive birdies," Lehman said.
Els was pleased with his performance after taking two weeks off following his U.S. Open win at Congressional.
"Finishing with a 66 completed a very nice week. I started very slowly, maybe too slowly, and gave Tom too much of a start for the way he is playing," Els said.
"It's all building up nicely for next week with Tom, myself, Greg Norman and Colin Montgomerie all playing well."
"This is a fabulous course and in an unbelievable setting," Els said.
Els will also have Tom Watson on his mind next week as he tries to become the first to win the U.S. and British Opens in the same year since the American did so in 1982.

Montgomerie, runner-up to Els at last month's U.S. Open, finished on minus eight after a 67 and said he plans a relaxed approach to next week's Open at Troon, where his father James is the club secretary.

The 34-year-old Scottish world number four, who has missed the halfway cut in four of the last five British Opens, said he might have only one practice round on the course which he has played since he was a boy.
